data.title: The legend of Modľatín – pagan fires on the hill of Žiar
data.excerpt: In the hills of Papradno and Mariková rises Kýčera, a hill 957 m high, and the valley of Modľatín stretches below it. A local legend explains the name of the valley: pagans burned their dead on a hill they called Žiar, and came here to pray for them.
data.metaTitle: The legend of Modľatín below Orgoňova Kýčera
data.metaDescription: A legend from the Modľatín valley below Orgoňova Kýčera (957 m) in the hills of Papradno and Mariková explains the names of Modľatín and Žiar hill.

timeline.title: Pagan burials on the hill of Žiar
timeline.description: Pagans cremated their dead on a hill which they named Žiar after the blazing pyres, and they went to pray for them at a place that thus received the name Modľatín.

children.text: In the hills of Papradno and Mariková there is one hill 957 m high, Kýčera, which the people of Mariková call Orgoňova Kýčera. Below it, on the northern side, stretches the valley of Modľatín (Modľacín), with hamlets of wooden cottages that once belonged to shepherds and have today been converted into holiday cabins. The Modľatínsky stream flows through the valley, gathering all the smaller brooks and rills. At the hamlet of Majer it flows into the Papradňanka. The surrounding countryside is beautiful: meadows full of flowers and, above all, deep, fragrant woods. On the steep hillside of Kýčera there is a very old wood, almost primeval, with mighty trees. They are chiefly beeches, marked by the ravages of time and by frequent gales. From time immemorial the wood has been called Starák, because there was always old forest there, which people avoided. Down from the forest, along the steep slope, runs a swift stream called Starákový. Between the roots of the trees and down to the hard rock it has cut a ravine and so created a magnificent scene – nothing but rapids and waterfalls over a length of about 100 m. And although the stream is not large, even with that little clear water its waterfalls are enchanting, especially in some places and above all in spring, when the snow is melting. Old legends say that beside the Starákový stream there is a hole – the entrance to a stone cellar in which a robbers' treasure lies hidden.
The legend about the origin of the name Modľatín runs as follows:

blocks.text: It was long, long ago, when there were as yet no Christians among us. Pagans lived here, who had various gods, honoured them and bowed down before them. They also buried their dead differently than we do today. They carried them right to the very top of a high hill, piled up a heap of wood and laid the dead man upon it. They even packed wood around him as well and then set it alight. The heaped, burning pyres blazed far into the distance, and that is why they named this hill Žiar, the Blaze. To pray for the buried – the cremated – dead they went to a place which thus received the name Modľatín, from modliť sa, to pray.
blocks.author: Santus
blocks.source: submitted by M. Portášík, recorded by Štefan Meliš (Polazník)

children.text: Who knows – perhaps one day, when archaeologists come to the place, something will be found to support this tradition.
